title: Stokes' Theorem
short_intro: Stokes' theorem relates the surface integral of the curl of a vector field over an open surface to the line integral of the vector field around the boundary curve of that surface. It serves as a higher-dimensional generalization of the Kelvin-Stokes theorem in vector calculus, fundamental for analyzing conservative fields and electromagnetic induction in mechanics and field theory.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Evaluation of line integrals in 2D and 3D, verification of conservative force fields, and simple applications relating work done by a force vector to curl evaluation.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous vector proofs, applications to fluid circulation, relation between differential and integral forms of Maxwell's equations, and Stokes' theorem in curvilinear or generalized coordinate systems.

concept_notes.heading: Statement of Stokes' Theorem
bullets: Let S be a piecewise smooth oriented open surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise smooth boundary curve C.
If vector field F possesses continuous first-order partial derivatives in an open region containing S, then the line integral of F along C equals the surface integral of the curl of F over S.
The orientation of C must be consistent with the surface normal vector n via the right-hand rule.

concept_notes.heading: Physical Interpretation of Curl
bullets: The curl of a vector field represents the infinitesimal circulation of the field at a point.
In mechanics, if F represents a velocity field of a fluid, the curl of F is proportional to the local vorticity or angular velocity vector of the fluid element.
A vector field is irrotational if and only if its curl is identically zero everywhere in the region.

concept_notes.heading: Relation to Conservative Forces
bullets: A central force field such as the gravitational force or an electrostatic force is conservative, implying that curl(F) = 0.
By Stokes' theorem, the line integral (work done) around any closed path C in a conservative field is zero, as the enclosed surface integral of curl(F) vanishes.
Path independence of line integrals is directly connected to the vanishing of the curl through Stokes' theorem.

concept_notes.heading: Orientation and Boundary Rules
bullets: The right-hand corkscrew rule defines the positive direction of the boundary curve C relative to the surface normal n.
If the fingers of the right hand curl in the direction of traversal along C, the thumb points in the direction of the unit normal vector n.
Reversing the orientation of the boundary curve C changes the sign of the resulting line integral.

derivations.title: Proof for Infinitesimal Rectangular Element
derivations.conditions: Applicable for a small rectangular surface element in the xy-plane bounded by dx and dy.
steps: Consider a rectangular loop in the xy-plane with vertices (x,y), (x+dx,y), (x+dx,y+dy), and (x,y+dy).
Evaluate the line integral of F = F_x i + F_y j around this closed loop by summing contributions along the four sides: int F.dr = F_x(x,y)dx + F_y(x+dx,y)dy - F_x(x,y+dy)dx - F_y(x,y)dy.
Rewrite the differences using partial derivatives: int F.dr = [F_y(x+dx,y) - F_y(x,y)]dy - [F_x(x,y+dy) - F_x(x,y)]dx = ( rac{partial F_y}{partial x} -  rac{partial F_x}{partial y}) dx dy.
Recognize the integrand as the z-component of the curl of F multiplied by the area element dA = dx dy.

derivations.title: Reduction of Surface Independence
derivations.conditions: For any two open surfaces S1 and S2 sharing the same oriented boundary curve C.
steps: Let S1 and S2 form a closed surface V by joining them along their common boundary C with opposite orientations.
Apply the divergence theorem or combine Stokes' theorem applications to show that the flux of curl(F) through the closed surface is zero.
Conclude that the surface integral depends solely on the boundary curve C and not on the specific choice of the open surface S spanning C, provided the field is continuously differentiable.

graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the geometric relationship between the 2D boundary curve C and the 3D surface S required for setting up Stokes' theorem limits.

graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A tiny paddle wheel placed in a swirling fluid velocity field v, where the axis of rotation aligns with the local curl vector (nabla cross v).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that the curl measures the axis and magnitude of local rotational tendency (vorticity) in a vector field.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently referenced in qualitative PGT questions regarding physical meaning of curl.

solved_numericals.question: Evaluate the line integral of the vector field F = y i + x j around the circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 in the xy-plane, traversed in the counterclockwise direction.
solution_steps: Identify the vector field components: F_x = y and F_y = x.
Compute the curl of F: \nabla \times \mathbf{F} = (\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}) \mathbf{k} = (1 - 1)\mathbf{k} = 0.
Apply Stokes' theorem: \oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{k} \, dS = \iint_S 0 \, dS = 0.

solved_numericals.question: Verify Stokes' theorem for the vector field F = -y^2 i + x j + z z k over the upper hemisphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 4, z >= 0, bounded by the circle x^2 + y^2 = 4 in the xy-plane.
solution_steps: Compute line integral: Parameterize the boundary circle C as x = 2 cos t, y = 2 sin t, z = 0 for t from 0 to 2\pi. Then d\mathbf{r} = (-2 \sin t \mathbf{i} + 2 \cos t \mathbf{j}) dt.
Evaluate \oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_0^{2\pi} [(-4 \sin^2 t)(-2 \sin t) + (2 \cos t)(2 \cos t)] dt = \int_0^{2\pi} (8 \sin^3 t + 4 \cos^2 t) dt = 0 + 4(\pi) = 4\pi.

Compute curl of F: \nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \\ -y^2 & x & z \end{vmatrix} = (0)\mathbf{i} + (0)\mathbf{j} + (1 - (-2y))\mathbf{k} = (1 + 2y)\mathbf{k}.

Evaluate surface integral: \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{n} \, dS = \iint_S (1 + 2y) \frac{z}{2} \, dS_{xy} over the disk x^2 + y^2 <= 4. Using polar coordinates, symmetry eliminates the 2y term, leaving \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2 1 \cdot r \, dr \, d\theta = \pi (2^2) = 4\pi.
Both integrals yield 4\pi, thus verifying Stokes' theorem.

solved_numericals.question: Using Stokes' theorem, evaluate \oint_C (y \mathbf{i} + z \mathbf{j} + x \mathbf{k}) \cdot d\mathbf{r} where C is the triangle with vertices (1,0,0), (0,1,0), and (0,0,1) oriented counterclockwise as viewed from the origin.
solution_steps: Identify F = y i + z j + x k.
The plane of the triangle is x + y + z = 1. The unit normal vector pointing upward is \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{3}}.
Calculate the area of the triangular surface S. The vertices give side vectors, yielding an area of \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The surface S must be orientable, meaning a consistent unit normal vector can be defined continuously across the entire surface.
The vector field F and its first-order partial derivatives must be continuous throughout an open region containing the surface S and its boundary C.
The theorem is restricted to 3D Euclidean space; higher-dimensional analogues require the generalized Stokes' theorem on differential forms.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Assuming Stokes' theorem applies only to flat surfaces in the xy-plane.
common_misconceptions.correct: Stokes' theorem applies to any piecewise smooth open orientable surface in 3D space bounded by curve C.
common_misconceptions.why: The surface can be curved, warped, or folded as long as it has a well-defined boundary curve and continuous normal.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Thinking the choice of surface S alters the value of the surface integral for a given boundary C.
common_misconceptions.correct: Any two surfaces sharing the same oriented boundary curve yield the exact same value for the surface integral of the curl.
common_misconceptions.why: Because the line integral depends solely on the boundary curve C, any surface spanning C gives identical results.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Ignoring the relative orientation between the curve C and surface normal n.
common_misconceptions.correct: Reversing the traversal direction of C flips the sign of the line integral.
common_misconceptions.why: Orientation consistency via the right-hand rule is mandatory for the equality in Stokes' theorem to hold.

quick_revision: Stokes' theorem connects the line integral around a closed boundary to the surface integral of the curl over the enclosed area: \oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{n} \, dS.
